title: Finite image of a projection fibre under a proper comparison after modifying the base
statement: Let $S$ be an integral Noetherian scheme [def-pc-integral-scheme] [pqf-def-locnoeth] with generic point $\eta$ and function field $K$. Let $C,X,Y$ be reduced schemes flat and of finite type over $S$ [def-weil-flat-morphism] [def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. Let $a:X\to C$ and $b:Y\to C$ be proper [def-weil-proper-morphism], isomorphisms on the generic fibres, and isomorphisms between schematically dense open subschemes. Here reduced means that the local rings have no nonzero nilpotents, and $j:U\hookrightarrow Z$ is schematically dense when $\mathcal O_Z\to j_*\mathcal O_U$ is injective. Suppose $Y$ is $\eta$-normal, meaning every finite [def-weil-finite-integral-morphism] $\eta$-modification of $Y$ is an isomorphism. Let $q:S'\to S$ be a proper birational morphism with $S'$ integral and function field $K$, inducing an isomorphism over a dense open of $S$. Put $X'=X\times_SS'$, $Y'=Y\times_SS'$, $C'=C\times_SS'$ [def-pc-fibre-product], and suppose that a $C'$-morphism $g:Y'\to X'$ is given. For every closed point $y\in Y$, let $s$ be its image in $S$; then $y$ is closed in the fibre $Y_s$ [def-pc-scheme-fibre]. Put $F=Y'\times_Y\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(y)$, with $\kappa(y)$ its residue field [def-weil-residue-field]. The image of the composite $F\to Y'\xrightarrow{g}X'\to X$ is a finite set of closed points of $X_s$. No valuation-comparison hypothesis is imposed.

source.place: Proposition 5.2 proof, printed p. 35, fibre-image subclaim before the use of connectedness. Temkin's printed inference (a closed subset of the relative closed-point locus is s-quasi-finite after projection) is invalid as written: a quasi-finite closed subset can be the graph of a nonconstant map. The subclaim is true under the flatness of X and Y over S assumed here; this node records only the statement.

proof.text: Fix the given closed point $y$ and its image $s$. Choose an affine neighbourhood of $s$ in $S$, then an affine neighbourhood $C_0$ of $b(y)$ inside its inverse image. Replace $C,X,Y$ by $C_0,a^{-1}(C_0),b^{-1}(C_0)$ and restrict $g$ accordingly. The entire fibre $F$ is retained, since its composite to $C$ is constantly $b(y)$. These restrictions remain reduced, flat and finite type; all opens involved are quasi-compact because finite-type schemes over the Noetherian base are Noetherian. Properness of $a,b$ survives the open base change. We may therefore assume $S=\operatorname{Spec}R$ and $C=\operatorname{Spec}A$ affine. In particular $X_s,Y_s$ are separated finite-type schemes over $\kappa(s)$, since they are proper over the affine scheme $C_s$.

source.place: Tags 01T6, 01W4; affine localization before applying Stein factorization (03H2).

proof.text: We will use schematic generic density explicitly. For a flat scheme over an integral base, on an affine chart over a domain every nonzero base element acts injectively on sections: apply the torsion-free sections lemma with the invertible module $\mathcal O$. Localization in these elements is therefore injective. This proves schematic density of the generic fibre. The same assertion holds after base change to $S'$: on affine charts, $(B\otimes_R R')\otimes_{R'}M=B\otimes_R M$ proves that base change preserves flatness, by applying the definition to injections of $R'$-modules. The affine criterion translates this back to schemes. We may also restrict to any open of the source. Consequently an ideal pulled back to one of these flat schemes is zero if its restriction to the generic fibre is zero.

source.place: Tags 01U5 and 01U9; injectivity of localization on flat sections. The explicit tensor argument establishes the base-change assertion.

proof.text: Index the irreducible components of $C_\eta$ by $i$, and put $n_i=\dim C_{i,\eta}$. The generic isomorphisms give corresponding components of $X_\eta$ and $Y_\eta$. Let $C_i,X_i,Y_i$ denote their reduced closures in the respective total spaces. Generic density from Step 2 and finiteness of the total component sets show that these are all total-space components: a component disjoint from the generic fibre would have a nonempty open away from the other finitely many components, contradicting density. Properness and the generic identifications give surjections $X_i\to C_i$ and $Y_i\to C_i$, since their closed images contain the generic point of $C_i$. The flat fibre-component-closure dimension theorem gives pure dimension $n_i$ for every nonempty fibre of each of $C_i,X_i,Y_i$. Its hypothesis concerns the ambient flat scheme, so no flatness of these reduced closures is asserted. Relative-dimension base change gives the same purity after every residue-field extension.

source.place: Tags 0GSJ (lemma-flat-associated-equidimensional), 02NK (lemma-base-change-relative-dimension-d), 01W1. Componentwise, with no common value of n_i assumed.

proof.text: Take the affine Stein factorization $Y\xrightarrow{p}D=\operatorname{Spec}B\xrightarrow{r}C$, where $B=\Gamma(Y,\mathcal O_Y)$. The affine Stein theorem makes $p$ proper, surjective, with geometrically connected fibres. Since $Y$ is locally Noetherian, $\mathcal O_Y$ is coherent; proper coherent cohomology over the Noetherian affine $C$ makes $B$ finite over $A$. Thus $r$ is finite. The ring $B$ is reduced, since sections on a reduced scheme have no nonzero nilpotents. Flat base change of global sections along $\operatorname{Spec}K\to\operatorname{Spec}R$ and $Y_\eta\simeq C_\eta$ give $B\otimes_RK\simeq A\otimes_RK$, with its canonical algebra map. Also $B\hookrightarrow B\otimes_RK$ by Step 2. Hence $D_\eta$ is dense in $D$: if $D(b)$ misses it, some power of $b$ is killed by a nonzero element of $R$, so $b$ is nilpotent and $D(b)$ is empty. Therefore the integral components $D_i$ of $D$ correspond to the same generic components, $D_i\to C_i$ is finite surjective, and $p(Y_i)=D_i$.

source.place: Tag 03H2 (theorem-stein-factorization-general); Coherent Tags 01XZ, 02O5, 02KH. Only the flat generic localization is used for global sections.

proof.text: The finite-dominant fibre-purity lemma applies to the finite dominant map r:D_i\to C_i. Since every nonempty fibre of C_i is pure of dimension n_i by Step 3, it gives that every nonempty fibre of D_i is pure of dimension n_i. Its proof uses the going-up description of components under an integral extension and the finite-surjective dimension theorem, so it does not infer a lower bound from openness of the bounded-dimension locus. The relative-dimension base-change theorem then gives the same purity after every field extension \Omega/\kappa(s).

source.place: Morphisms Tag 02FZ (lemma-openness-bounded-dimension-fibres), Varieties Tag 0A21, Algebra Tag 00OK; Morphisms Tag 02NK. Expanded finite-cover dimension argument.

proof.text: Choose an algebraic closure $\Omega$ of $\kappa(s)$ and write $T=S'\times_S\operatorname{Spec}\Omega$. It is proper and finite type over $\Omega$. The fibre of $g$ gives $H:T\times_\Omega Y_\Omega\to X_\Omega$, over $C_\Omega$, by forgetting its $T$ coordinate. Here the subscript $\Omega$ means base change from $S$ through $s$. All these schemes are Noetherian. If $T$ is empty the required image is empty. Otherwise let $W$ be any connected component of $Y_\Omega$; it is open and closed, since a Noetherian scheme has finitely many irreducible components and its connected components are their disjoint maximal connected unions. We will prove finiteness of the image of $T\times\{z\}$ for every $\Omega$-rational point $z\in W$.

source.place: Tag 01W4 and Noetherian finite-type permanence; geometric special-fibre product and its connected components.

proof.text: Under $p_\Omega$, the component $W$ is exactly the inverse image of a connected component $V$ of $D_\Omega$. Indeed $p_\Omega$ is a closed surjection with connected nonempty fibres. It is a quotient map, and the connected-preimage theorem makes the inverse image of each closed connected component of $D_\Omega$ connected; maximality of connected components gives the assertion. Since $p:Y_i\to D_i$ is proper surjective, so is its base change to $\Omega$. Thus $W$ meets $(Y_i)_\Omega$ exactly when $V$ meets $(D_i)_\Omega$. Choose $n$ maximal among the $n_i$ with this property, and choose one such $i$. A component $E$ of $(D_i)_\Omega$ meeting $V$ lies entirely in $V$, since $V$ is open and closed. It has dimension $n$ by Step 5. Its finite image $B_0\subseteq (C_i)_\Omega$, with reduced structure, is integral and has dimension $n$.

source.place: Stein Tag 03H2; Topology Tag 0377 (lemma-connected-fibres-quotient-topology-connected-components); Algebra Tag 00OK.

proof.text: Let $X_{\leq n}\subseteq X$ be the reduced union of the $X_j$ with $n_j\leq n$, and let $Y^0=Y\setminus\bigcup_{n_j>n}Y_j$. By the maximality defining $n$, $W\subseteq Y^0_\Omega$. On the generic fibre the comparison $g$ is forced to equal $a_\eta^{-1}b_\eta$, so its restriction to $(Y^0)'$ lands in $(X_{\leq n})'$. This holds scheme-theoretically on the entire $(Y^0)'$: pull back the ideal of $(X_{\leq n})'$; it is zero generically, and Step 2 makes it zero everywhere because $(Y^0)'$ is flat over the integral $S'$. Hence $H|_{T\times W}$ lands in $(X_{\leq n})_\Omega$. This step only uses the displayed ideal argument; it does not infer factorization through a closed subscheme from pointwise containment.

source.place: Temkin Proposition 5.2 comparison diagram; schematic generic density from flatness, as proved in Step 2.

proof.text: Put $P=(X_{\leq n})_\Omega\times_{C_\Omega}B_0$. It is proper over the integral $B_0$ and has dimension at most $n$: it is closed in $(X_{\leq n})_\Omega$, because $B_0$ is closed in $C_\Omega$, and Step 3 bounds every component of the latter scheme by $n$. If an integral component $L$ of $P$ dominates $B_0$, the closed-dominant dimension formula gives $\dim L=\dim B_0+\operatorname{trdeg}_{\kappa(B_0)}\kappa(L)$. Thus $\dim L=n$ and this transcendence degree is zero. The generic fibre of $L\to B_0$ is integral, proper and finite type over $\kappa(B_0)$, and applying that same dimension formula over this field makes it zero-dimensional. It is a finite set by the zero-dimensional closed-subset lemma. A nondominating component of $P$ has closed image missing the generic point of $B_0$. There are finitely many components, so the whole generic fibre of $P\to B_0$ is finite.

source.place: Morphisms Tag 02JX (lemma-alteration-dimension), applied to each proper dominating component and then to its generic fibre; finite-component argument.

proof.text: The proper finite-fibre neighbourhood theorem, applied to $P\to B_0$ at the generic point of the Noetherian $B_0$, supplies a nonempty open $U\subseteq B_0$ over which $P$ is finite. Choose a closed point $e$ of the nonempty open $E\times_{B_0}U$ and then a closed point $z_0$ of its nonempty inverse image in $(Y_i)_\Omega$. Such points exist by choosing a maximal ideal on a nonempty affine chart; their residue fields are $\Omega$ by the closed-point field theorem, and the same theorem makes them closed in the ambient finite-type schemes. They lie in $V$ and $W$ respectively. Put $c_0=b(z_0)\in U$. Finite morphisms have finite fibres by the finite-closed-map theorem. Step 8 implies that $H(T\times\{z_0\})$ is contained in the finite fibre $P_{c_0}$, viewed in $X_\Omega$. We have therefore found an actual rational seed point of $W$ with finite image.

source.place: Cohomology of Schemes Tag 02OH (lemma-proper-finite-fibre-finite-in-neighbourhood); Morphisms Tags 01WN, 02NU, 02NH for finite fibres; Tag 01TB for rational closed points.

proof.text: Cover $T$ by the reduced closed subschemes $T_1,\ldots,T_m$ underlying its irreducible components. Each is integral, nonempty, proper and finite type over $\Omega$. It has a rational closed point by the closed-point field theorem, so the connected-point geometric-connectedness criterion makes it geometrically connected. It is geometrically reduced by the perfect-field reducedness theorem: an algebraically closed field is perfect, since in positive characteristic every $a$ has a root of $t^p-a$. The finite image of $T_r\times\{z_0\}$ in Step 10 is connected. Its points are closed: each has residue field algebraic over $\Omega$, because the image lies in the finite fibre over the rational $c_0$. The closed-point field theorem therefore makes that image a finite discrete set. A nonempty connected finite discrete set is a singleton.

Apply the rigidity lemma to the proper geometrically connected geometrically reduced $\Omega$-scheme $T_r$, the connected $\Omega$-scheme $W$, and the separated finite-type target $X_\Omega$, using the morphism $H|_{T_r\times W}$ and the rational point $z_0\in W$. Step 11 supplies its singleton-image hypothesis. It follows that $H|_{T_r\times W}$ factors through $W$. Consequently for every rational $z\in W$, the image of $T_r\times\{z\}$ is a single rational point of $X_\Omega$; rationality follows by evaluating at a rational point of $T_r$. The finite component cover remains surjective after product with $W$, so $H(T\times\{z\})$ is the union of at most $m$ such points. This proves the assertion for every rational point on every connected component of $Y_\Omega$. Nilpotents in $T$ do not affect the argument: the component cover by the reductions is universally surjective and covers all points of this product.

source.place: Mumford rigidity in the existing lem-sc-rigidity; Temkin fibre-image subclaim repaired by applying rigidity to each proper parameter component.

proof.text: Since $y$ is closed in the finite-type $\kappa(s)$-scheme $Y_s$, the field $\kappa(y)$ is finite over $\kappa(s)$. Thus $\operatorname{Spec}(\kappa(y)\otimes_{\kappa(s)}\Omega)$ has finitely many points, all with residue field $\Omega$: indeed for any prime its quotient is a finite-dimensional domain, hence a field (multiplication by a nonzero element is injective and therefore surjective); so the spectrum is zero-dimensional and the zero-dimensional closed-subset lemma makes it finite. Its residue fields are finite over the algebraically closed $\Omega$. The corresponding rational points of $Y_\Omega$ lie on finitely many components $W$. The geometric base change of $F$ is $T\times_\Omega\operatorname{Spec}(\kappa(y)\otimes_{\kappa(s)}\Omega)$. Its underlying space is covered by the finitely many products $T\times\{z\}$ above those rational points. Step 12 therefore gives a finite set of rational points as its image in $X_\Omega$. Surjectivity of field extension (on a fibre-product point choose a prime in the nonzero tensor product of the two residue fields) implies that this image projects onto the original image in $X_s$. Each projected point has residue field algebraic over $\kappa(s)$, since it embeds into its rational lifting's field $\Omega$. The closed-point field theorem makes every such point closed in $X_s$. This proves exactly the required finite set of closed points.

source.place: Varieties Tag 01TB; Algebra, finite-dimensional algebras over a field; Schemes Tag 01JT for points of fibre products. Final geometric-to-ordinary image argument.

proof_origin.place: Temkin Proposition 5.2, printed p. 35, provides the diagram but its projection inference is insufficient. Agent-written repair by componentwise flat fibre dimensions (0GSJ), affine Stein factorization (03H2), dimension theory (02FZ, 02JX), and the existing Mumford rigidity lemma.

lean.statement: theorem base_modification_comparison_fibre_image {S : Scheme.{u}} [IsIntegral S] [IsNoetherian S] (η : S) (hη : IsGenericPoint η Set.univ) {C X Y : Scheme.{u}} (c : C ⟶ S) (x : X ⟶ S) (y : Y ⟶ S) [Flat c] [Flat x] [Flat y] [LocallyOfFiniteType c] [QuasiCompact c] [LocallyOfFiniteType x] [QuasiCompact x] [LocallyOfFiniteType y] [QuasiCompact y] [IsReduced C] [IsReduced X] [IsReduced Y] (a : X ⟶ C) (b : Y ⟶ C) (hac : a ≫ c = x) (hbc : b ≫ c = y) (ha : EtaModification (S.fromSpecStalk η) a c) (hb : EtaModification (S.fromSpecStalk η) b c) (hnormal : ∀ {Z : Scheme.{u}} (f : Z ⟶ Y), IsFinite f → EtaModification (S.fromSpecStalk η) f (b ≫ c) → IsIso f) {S' : Scheme.{u}} (q : S' ⟶ S) [IsIntegral S'] (hq : IsProper q) (hbirational : ∃ U : S.Opens, Dense (U : Set S) ∧ IsIso (q ∣_ U)) (g : pullback y q ⟶ pullback x q) (hgq : g ≫ pullback.snd x q = pullback.snd y q) (hgc : g ≫ pullback.fst x q ≫ a = pullback.fst y q ≫ b) (hy : Y) (hyclosed : IsClosed ({y.asFiber hy} : Set (y.fiber (y hy)))) : (Set.range (baseModificationFibreMap c x y a b hac hbc q g hgc hy)).Finite ∧ ∀ z ∈ Set.range (baseModificationFibreMap c x y a b hac hbc q g hgc hy), IsClosed ({z} : Set (x.fiber (y hy)))
